question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Mischievious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correctly spelt word is "Mischievous" (not "Mischievious") — meaning causing or showing a playful desire to tease or cause trouble. (शरारती)
◦ Example: The mischievous child hid his sister's shoes as a prank.

• Spelling rule: the word ends in -vous, not -vious. A very common error is inserting an extra "i" before "ous" (mischiev + i + ous), which is wrong; the correct ending directly attaches "-ous" to "mischiev-".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Conscientious" is correctly spelt — meaning wishing to do one's work or duty well and thoroughly. (कर्तव्यनिष्ठ)

• Option 3: "Ostentatious" is correctly spelt — meaning characterized by vulgar or pretentious display, designed to impress. (दिखावटी)

• Option 4: "Accommodate" is correctly spelt — note the double "c" and double "m", meaning to provide lodging or sufficient space for. (समायोजित करना)

NOTE

• Other words commonly misspelt in the same way as "mischievous" (wrongly given an extra "i"): grievous (not grievious), outrageous (not outrageious).

• Remember: "mischievous" has only THREE syllables (mis-chie-vous), not four — that is why there is no "i" before "-ous".

question:
Select the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank.
Helium is used with oxygen for asthma treatment because it _____________ very easily.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. diffuses.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "diffuses" — the third person singular present tense of "diffuse", meaning to spread out or become dispersed gradually in a gas or liquid.
◦ Example: A drop of ink diffuses quickly when placed in a glass of water.

• Spelling key: DIF + FUSE + S. Note the double "f" and the ending "-fuse" (not "-fuze" or "-fusez"). The word comes from the Latin diffundere, meaning "to pour out, spread".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "difusez" — incorrect; missing one "f" and wrongly ends in "-ez".

• Option 2: "difuses" — incorrect; the double "f" is missing (should be "ff").

• Option 4: "diffuzes" — incorrect; the "s" in "-fuse" has been wrongly replaced with a "z".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "diffuse" (to spread out) with "defuse" (to remove the fuse from a bomb, or to make a situation less tense) — both are frequently tested for spelling and usage in SSC exams.

• Other words with the double "ff" pattern that are commonly tested: affect, effect, offer, suffer, differ.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Exceptional
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Outstanding.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Exceptional" means unusual, remarkable, or far above average in quality or ability. (असाधारण, उत्कृष्ट)
◦ Example: She showed exceptional talent in mathematics at a very young age.

• "Outstanding" means exceptionally good, or clearly noticeable because of excellence, which matches the meaning of "exceptional" closely. (उत्कृष्ट, विशिष्ट)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Trivial" means unimportant or of little value — this is nearly opposite in sense to "exceptional".

• Option 2: "Emotional" means relating to a person's feelings — unrelated to the idea of being remarkable.

• Option 3: "Total" means complete or entire in amount or degree — it does not carry the sense of excellence.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "exceptional" useful for SSC exams: extraordinary, remarkable, exemplary, phenomenal, unparalleled.

• Antonyms of "exceptional": ordinary, mediocre, average, common.

question: Select the sentence in which the ‘-ing’ form of verb expresses the continuity of an action/event.
option_1: Reading novels is my favourite pastime.
option_2: I am fond of reading science fiction.
option_3: Please do not disturb me. I am preparing for exams.
option_4: The optician advised me to use reading glasses.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Please do not disturb me. I am preparing for exams.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The '-ing' form of a verb can function in different ways — as a gerund (noun), as a participle adjective, or as part of the continuous/progressive tense, where it expresses an action that is still going on at the time of speaking.

• Rule — Present Continuous Tense: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing, used for an action that is happening right now or around the present moment and is not yet complete.

• In "I am preparing for exams", the verb "preparing" is part of the present continuous tense "am preparing", showing that the action of preparing is ongoing/continuing at the moment of speaking.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Reading novels is my favourite pastime" — here "Reading" is a gerund acting as the subject of the sentence, not expressing continuity of an ongoing action.

• Option 2: "I am fond of reading science fiction" — here "reading" is a gerund used as the object of the preposition "of"; it names an activity in general, not an action in progress.

• Option 4: "The optician advised me to use reading glasses" — here "reading" is used as a participle adjective describing the noun "glasses" (i.e., glasses meant for reading), not a continuous action.

NOTE

• An '-ing' word can be a gerund (noun: Swimming is fun), a present participle in continuous tense (action ongoing: She is swimming), or a participle adjective (describing a noun: a swimming pool). SSC frequently tests the ability to distinguish these three uses.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who eats the flesh of his own species
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cannibal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Cannibal" is one who eats the flesh of his own species (a human who eats human flesh, or an animal that eats members of its own kind). (नरभक्षी)
◦ Example: The documentary described how certain species of spiders behave as cannibals, eating members of their own kind.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Non-vegetarian" means one who eats meat/flesh of other species in general, not specifically of one's own species.

• Option 2: "Vegan" means one who does not eat or use any animal products at all — the opposite sense.

• Option 4: "Mammal" refers to a class of warm-blooded animals that feed their young with milk — it has nothing to do with eating habits.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions frequently asked by SSC: Carnivorous (flesh-eating animal), Herbivorous (plant-eating animal), Omnivorous (eating both plants and flesh), Vegetarian (one who eats no meat).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The appearance of most of the animals in jungle is deceptive in nature.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. honest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "deceptive" means giving an appearance or impression different from the true one; misleading. (भ्रामक, धोखा देने वाला)

• The antonym of "deceptive" is "honest", meaning free of deceit; truthful and sincere; giving a true impression. (ईमानदार, सच्चा)
◦ Example: Unlike the deceptive camouflage of the chameleon, the peacock's honest display of colour is meant to attract attention.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "illusive" means based on illusion, misleading — this is actually a synonym, not an antonym, of "deceptive".

• Option 3: "ugly" means unpleasant to look at — this relates to appearance in general, not to truthfulness, so it is not the opposite of "deceptive".

• Option 4: "beautiful" means pleasing to look at — again, this concerns aesthetics, not truthfulness, so it does not express the opposite of "misleading".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "illusive" (misleading, based on illusion) with "elusive" (difficult to find or catch) — both are commonly tested in SSC vocabulary questions.

• Other synonyms of "deceptive": misleading, deceitful, fallacious, illusory. Other antonyms: genuine, sincere, truthful.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Dipesh will send Rakesh away to college for certain reasons.
option_1: Rakesh will have to be sent away to college for certain reasons by Dipesh.
option_2: Rakesh will be sent away to college for certain reasons by Dipesh.
option_3: Rakesh would have been sent away to college for certain reasons by Dipesh.
option_4: Rakesh would be sent away to college for certain reasons by Dipesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Rakesh will be sent away to college for certain reasons by Dipesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Dipesh will send Rakesh away to college for certain reasons" is in the Simple Future Tense.

• Rule — Simple Future Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + will/shall + V1 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + will/shall + be + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "Rakesh" becomes the subject; the auxiliary "will" is retained and followed by "be"; the main verb "send" becomes its past participle "sent"; and "Dipesh" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: Rakesh will be sent away to college for certain reasons by Dipesh.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "will have to be sent" wrongly introduces the idea of obligation/necessity, which is not present in the original active sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "would have been sent" is the passive form associated with a conditional/past perfect construction, not the simple future tense of the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "would be sent" uses "would", which changes the tense to a conditional/hypothetical sense instead of keeping the simple future "will".

NOTE

• When converting active to passive, the tense of the auxiliary verb must be preserved exactly — only the voice (structure) changes, not the tense.

• Adverbials of manner/place such as "away to college" and reason phrases such as "for certain reasons" remain unchanged in position after the main verb in the passive sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The long-standing feud between the two villages was settled due to the intervention of the two chiefs.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Harmony.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "feud" means a prolonged and bitter quarrel or dispute, especially a long-standing one between families, individuals or groups. (झगड़ा, वैमनस्य)

• The antonym of "feud" is "harmony", meaning a state of peaceful agreement and cooperation; concord. (सामंजस्य, मेल-मिलाप)
◦ Example: After years of feud, the two families finally lived in harmony.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Humility" means the quality of having a modest or low view of one's own importance — unrelated to conflict or peace between two parties.

• Option 3: "Humble" is an adjective meaning modest or unpretentious — again unrelated to the idea of dispute versus peace.

• Option 4: "Honesty" means the quality of being truthful and sincere — it does not express the opposite of a quarrel.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "feud": conflict, dispute, vendetta, rivalry, animosity. Other antonyms: peace, accord, agreement, reconciliation.

• Related word: "feud" as a verb means to carry on a bitter, prolonged quarrel (e.g., "The two clans have feuded for generations").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Forsake
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Abandon.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Forsake" means to give up or leave someone/something entirely, especially in violation of a promise or duty; to desert. (त्यागना, छोड़ देना)
◦ Example: He would never forsake his friends in times of trouble.

• "Abandon" means to give up completely or desert someone/something, which closely matches the meaning of "forsake". (त्याग देना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Accelerate" means to increase in speed — unrelated in meaning to "forsake".

• Option 2: "Reveal" means to make known or disclose something previously hidden — unrelated to abandoning something.

• Option 4: "Clutch" means to grasp or hold tightly — this is actually close to the opposite of "forsake" (to let go of).

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "forsake": desert, renounce, relinquish, ditch, jilt.

• Antonyms of "forsake": embrace, cherish, retain, uphold.

question:
Select the most appropriate homophone to fill in the blank.
He _________ his bike as fast as he could to reach home.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. rode.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires the past tense of the verb "ride", since the sentence describes a completed action of riding a bike in the past ("as fast as he could to reach home").

• "Rode" is the simple past tense of "ride" (ride – rode – ridden), meaning to have travelled on/controlled a vehicle such as a bicycle, motorbike, or horse.
◦ Example: She rode her bicycle to school every day last year.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "road" is a noun meaning a wide way leading from one place to another — it is a homophone of "rode" but cannot function as a verb in this sentence.

• Option 3: "rowed" is the past tense of "row" (to propel a boat with oars) — it does not fit the context of riding a bike.

• Option 4: "rote" means a mechanical or habitual repetition of something (as in "learning by rote") — it is unrelated in meaning and does not fit grammatically.

NOTE

• Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning. Other commonly confused homophone sets tested by SSC: write/right/rite, their/there/they're, peace/piece, stationary/stationery.

• Always check the part of speech required by the sentence (verb, noun, etc.) when choosing between homophones.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Sivamani is working as an electrician for the past 22 years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. has been working.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "for the past 22 years" indicates an action that began in the past and is still continuing up to the present moment — this is the hallmark of the Present Perfect Continuous Tense, not the Present Continuous Tense used in the original sentence.

• Rule — Present Perfect Continuous Tense: Subject + has/have + been + V-ing (+ for/since + time expression), used for an action that started in the past and is still going on.

• Since the subject "Sivamani" is singular (third person), the auxiliary must be "has", giving "has been working".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "had been worked" is grammatically wrong — it wrongly mixes the past perfect continuous auxiliary "had been" with a passive-like "worked", and "had been" is used for an action completed before another past action, not for an action continuing to the present.

• Option 3: "have been working" is incorrect because the auxiliary "have" is used with plural subjects or "I/you/we/they", not with the singular third-person subject "Sivamani", which requires "has".

• Option 4: "would work" expresses a conditional or habitual past action, not an action continuing from the past into the present, so it does not fit "for the past 22 years".

NOTE

• Time expressions like "for + a period" (for 22 years) and "since + a point in time" (since 2002) are strong signals for the Present Perfect / Present Perfect Continuous tense.

• Present Perfect Continuous emphasises the duration and continuity of an action, while Present Perfect simply emphasises its completion or result.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill the blank in the given situation.
I thought Sadhna would always stick by me, but when I got into trouble, she turned out to be a/an ____________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. fair-weather friend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "fair-weather friend" means a person who is a friend only when things are going well, but who deserts you in times of trouble or difficulty. (मतलबी दोस्त, केवल सुख में साथ देने वाला मित्र)
◦ Example: He proved to be a fair-weather friend, disappearing the moment I needed help.

• The context of the sentence — Sadhna failing to stand by the speaker "when I got into trouble" — exactly matches this idiom's meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hard nut to crack" (मुश्किल काम/व्यक्ति): a person or problem that is very difficult to deal with or understand.

• Option 2: "open secret" (खुला रहस्य): something that is supposed to be a secret but is actually known to many people.

• Option 4: "white elephant" (महंगी परन्तु बेकार वस्तु): a possession that is expensive to maintain but of little use or value.

NOTE

• Other idioms about friendship/loyalty often asked in SSC: "to stab someone in the back" (to betray), "through thick and thin" (in good times and bad), "to turn one's back on someone" (to abandon).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined word segment in the given sentence.
Her thinning grey hair was hanging on her bony forehead.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. straggling over.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Straggling over" means spreading out or growing untidily and unevenly over a surface, which fits the image of thin, sparse grey hair spread loosely and irregularly over the forehead. (बिखरा हुआ फैलना)
◦ Example: A few strands of straggling hair fell over her wrinkled forehead.

• The underlined phrase "hanging on" in this context describes hair drooping loosely and untidily over the forehead, a sense best captured by "straggling over".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "falling about" (बेतरतीब गिरना): usually used for people falling about with laughter, or objects scattered carelessly — it does not fit the description of thin hair on a forehead.

• Option 2: "urging ahead" (आगे बढ़ने के लिए प्रेरित करना): means pushing forward or encouraging progress — entirely unrelated to hair or physical description.

• Option 4: "sinking from" (डूबना): means going down or submerging — it does not describe hair hanging over a forehead.

NOTE

• "Straggle" as a verb can describe hair, plants, or even people/groups spreading out in a disorganised way (e.g., "a few straggling houses along the road").

• Commonly confused with "struggle" (to make a great effort) — note the spelling difference: strAggle vs strUggle.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined segment.
My father always tells amusing and true stories from his childhood at bedtime.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. anecdotes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "anecdote" is a short, amusing or interesting story about a real incident or person, often told to illustrate a point. (किस्सा, संस्मरण)
◦ Example: The teacher shared an anecdote from his college days to make the lecture interesting.

• The underlined phrase "amusing and true stories" exactly matches the definition of "anecdotes" — both "amusing" and "true" (based on real incidents) are captured by this single word.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "sonnets" are a specific form of 14-line poem — unrelated to true stories.

• Option 3: "fables" are short stories, typically with animal characters, meant to teach a moral lesson — they are fictional, not true, so they do not fit "true stories".

• Option 4: "allegories" are stories, poems, or pictures that use symbolic characters/events to reveal a hidden moral or political meaning — again fictional/symbolic, not real accounts.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often tested by SSC: Autobiography (one's own life story written by oneself), Biography (life story of a person written by someone else), Memoir (a personal account of remembered events), Chronicle (a factual record of events in order of time).

question:
Select the option that spots the error in the use of preposition in the given sentence.
Deepa and Seema are both good with running, but Deepa is also good at catching the ball and throwing it to the right corner in time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. good with running.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct preposition to use after the adjective "good" when referring to skill or ability at an activity is "at", not "with".

• Rule: "Good" takes the preposition "at" when followed by an activity/skill (good at singing, good at cricket, good at running). "With" is used with "good" typically when referring to how one handles people or objects/tools (e.g., "good with children", "good with tools").

• Since "running" is an activity/skill (like catching the ball, which correctly uses "at" later in the same sentence), the phrase should read "good at running", not "good with running".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to the right corner." is correct — "throw something to a place" correctly uses the preposition "to".

• Option 2: "at catching the ball" is correct — "good at" + gerund is the standard correct structure, exactly as it should also be used for "running".

• Option 4: "in time" is correct — the idiomatic phrase "in time" (meaning early enough) is correctly used here.

NOTE

• Common "adjective + preposition" combinations tested by SSC: good at, fond of, afraid of, interested in, angry with (a person), angry at (a thing/situation), good with (people/tools).

• Watch for sentences that use two different (and inconsistent) prepositions with the same adjective for parallel ideas, as seen here with "good with running" vs. "good at catching".

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
An intense wish to learn something keeps the nerves active.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. powerful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "intense" means existing in an extreme degree; very strong, forceful, or deeply felt. (तीव्र, प्रबल)
◦ Example: She felt an intense desire to travel the world.

• "Powerful" means having great strength or force, which closely matches the sense of "intense" as used here (a very strong wish). (शक्तिशाली, प्रबल)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "fixed" means firmly attached or unchanging — it describes stability, not intensity/strength.

• Option 3: "lazy" means unwilling to work or use effort — this is nearly opposite to the energetic sense of "intense".

• Option 4: "half-hearted" means lacking enthusiasm or effort — again nearly opposite to "intense", which suggests strong enthusiasm.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "intense": fierce, extreme, acute, ardent, fervent.

• Antonyms of "intense": mild, weak, moderate, half-hearted.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the idiom in the given brackets.
His PhD degree seems to be (Penelope's web).
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. An endless task.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Penelope's web" means a task that is never finished; an endless or interminable piece of work. (कभी न समाप्त होने वाला कार्य)
◦ Example: Writing this dictionary has become a Penelope's web — every time we finish a section, new words need to be added.

• The idiom originates from Greek mythology: Penelope, wife of Odysseus, wove a burial shroud by day and secretly unravelled it every night to delay having to choose a new husband from her suitors — so the work was never actually completed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "An important task" does not capture the sense of endlessness central to the idiom.

• Option 2: "A difficult task" describes difficulty, not the specific idea of a task that never ends.

• Option 3: "A secret task" is unrelated to the meaning; the idiom is about endlessness, not secrecy.

NOTE

• Other mythology/literature-based idioms tested by SSC: "Achilles' heel" (a weak or vulnerable point), "Herculean task" (a task requiring great strength/effort), "Pandora's box" (a source of many unforeseen troubles), "Sword of Damocles" (an imminent, ever-present danger).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the underlined group of words.
Humour that describes the weaknesses of the other person is itself a crime among peer groups.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Satire.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Satire" is the use of humour, irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to criticise or expose a person's vices, follies, or weaknesses. (व्यंग्य)
◦ Example: The cartoonist used satire to mock the corrupt politician's broken promises.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A joke" is simply something said or done to cause amusement — it need not specifically target another person's weaknesses.

• Option 2: "Attire" means clothing or dress — completely unrelated in meaning; it is likely included only because it sounds similar to "satire".

• Option 4: "A curse" means a solemn appeal for harm to befall someone, or an expression of profanity — this does not mean humour based on weaknesses.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often tested by SSC: Sarcasm (a cutting, often ironic remark meant to hurt or mock), Irony (expressing meaning through language that normally signifies the opposite), Parody (an imitation of a work meant to mock or amuse), Caricature (an exaggerated, often comic depiction of a person's features).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Why are you repeatedly called by her?
option_2: Why had she called you repeatedly?
option_3: Why was she calling you repeatedly?
option_4: Why does she call you repeatedly?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Why does she call you repeatedly?

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Why are you repeatedly called by her?" is a passive voice interrogative sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense (interrogative, wh-word):
◦ Passive: Wh-word + am/is/are + Subject(old object) + V3 + by + Object(old subject)?
◦ Active: Wh-word + do/does + Subject(new, old agent) + V1 + Object(new, old subject)?

• Applying the rule: the agent "her" becomes the subject "she"; since "she" is third person singular, the auxiliary is "does"; the past participle "called" becomes the base verb "call"; and "you" (originally the subject) becomes the object.
◦ Active: Why does she call you repeatedly?

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Why she calls you repeatedly?" is incorrect because a question requires the auxiliary "does" before the subject ("Why does she call..."); this option lacks the necessary subject-auxiliary inversion.

• Option 2: "Why had she called you repeatedly?" wrongly changes the tense to Past Perfect, which is not present in the original sentence.

• Option 3: "Why was she calling you repeatedly?" wrongly changes the tense to Past Continuous, instead of retaining the Simple Present Tense of the original.

NOTE

• When converting a passive interrogative sentence beginning with a wh-word to active voice, the auxiliary do/does/did must be correctly placed right after the wh-word, and it must agree with the new (converted) subject.

• Always preserve the original tense while changing voice — only the sentence structure (who acts vs. who is acted upon) should change.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Autonomy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Dependence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Autonomy" means the right or condition of self-government; freedom from external control or influence; independence. (स्वायत्तता, स्वशासन)

• The antonym of "autonomy" is "Dependence", meaning the state of relying on or being controlled by someone or something else. (निर्भरता, परावलंबन)
◦ Example: The colony's fight for autonomy ended its long dependence on the ruling power.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Permanence" means the state of lasting or remaining unchanged indefinitely — unrelated to the idea of self-rule versus control by others.

• Option 3: "Independence" is actually a synonym, not an antonym, of "autonomy" — both mean freedom from external control.

• Option 4: "Economical" means giving good value for the money spent, or thrifty — unrelated in meaning to "autonomy".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "autonomy": self-governance, self-rule, sovereignty, independence.

• Other antonyms of "autonomy": subjugation, subordination, subjection.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The limbs of the flying squirrel are interlinked with a membrane. When the creature (1)_________ into the air, the membrane opens and the squirrel seems to (2)_______ swiftly downwards. This movement gives the (3)_______ of flight. However, it is not flying really. It is a (4)_______ in the air from a higher level. It is also noteworthy that a squirrel cannot (5)_____ its direction while it is in flying mode.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. leaps.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the flying squirrel's action of jumping "into the air" — the verb that best fits this sense is "leaps", meaning to jump or spring a long distance, or high up, with great force.

• Grammatically, since the subject "the creature" is third person singular and the passage is in the Simple Present Tense (used for describing general facts/habitual behaviour), the verb must take the "-s" ending: "leaps".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "spring" is close in meaning (to jump suddenly) but is grammatically wrong here since it lacks the required "-s" ending for third-person singular subject agreement (it should be "springs").

• Option 2: "cross" means to go from one side to another — it does not convey the idea of jumping into the air, and it also lacks the "-s" ending.

• Option 3: "hurdle" means to jump over an obstacle — it implies clearing a barrier, which is not the sense intended (jumping into the air), and it too lacks subject-verb agreement.

NOTE

• In cloze passages describing general/habitual facts (like animal behaviour), the Simple Present Tense is used, and third-person singular subjects always require the verb to end in "-s"/"-es" — check this agreement carefully while eliminating options.

• Synonyms of "leap": jump, spring, bound, hop.

• The blank completes the sentence **"a squirrel cannot ___ its direction while it is in flying mode" — the word needed means to change or switch one thing for another, which is best expressed by "swap"**.

• The sentence is stating a limitation: once gliding, the squirrel cannot change/switch its direction mid-air (unlike a bird, which can steer using flapping wings).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "adopt" means to choose to take up or start using something (such as a plan, child, or habit) — it does not mean to change direction.

• Option 2: "replace" means to take the place of something or put something new in the place of another — while related to the idea of change, it does not idiomatically pair with "direction" the way "swap" (change/switch) does in this context.

• Option 3: "adept" is an adjective meaning highly skilled or proficient — it cannot grammatically function as a verb after "cannot", so it does not fit the sentence structure at all.

NOTE

• "Swap" as a verb means to exchange or switch one thing for another; here it is used to mean changing course/direction while gliding.

• The passage overall highlights a real biological limitation of flying squirrels: once launched into a glide, they have limited ability to alter course, unlike powered fliers such as birds and bats.
